“SLB delivered solid third-quarter results with all regions growing sequentially — led by a gradual recovery in the Middle East, growth in North America land and broadening international activity in deepwater offshore basins,” said SLB Chief Executive Officer Olivier Le Peuch.
Revenue growth

Cyclical sectors like energy often flatter weaker operators during favorable price environments, but a longer-term lens separates those from businesses that can consistently perform across market cycles. Over the last five years, SLB grew its revenue at a decent 10.7% compounded annual growth rate. Its growth was slightly above the average energy upstream and integrated energy company and shows its offerings resonate with customers.

Within energy, a single time frame, even a long one, only sheds light on how well a company rode the last commodity cycle. An even longer, ten-year view helps assess whether a company compounds through cycles. SLB’s annualized revenue growth of 2.6% over the last ten years is below its five-year trend, but the results were still good.
This quarter, SLB reported year-on-year revenue growth of 5.8%, and its $9.45 billion of revenue exceeded Wall Street’s consensus estimates by 1.7%.
Adjusted EBITDA margin

Adjusted EBITDA margin measures the operating profitability of an energy producer by excluding accounting effects related to depletion and capitalized drilling costs. It reveals how much cash the asset base generates before capital structure and reinvestment requirements shape reported earnings.
SLB was profitable over the last five years but held back by its large cost base. Its average EBITDA margin of 23% was weak for an upstream and integrated energy business.

Looking at the trend in its profitability, SLB’s EBITDA margin might have fluctuated slightly but has generally stayed the same over the last year. This raises questions about the company’s expense base because its revenue growth should have given it leverage on its fixed costs, resulting in better economies of scale and profitability.

This quarter, SLB reported an EBITDA margin of 24.8%, up 1.7 percentage points year on year. The improvement indicates greater efficiency. Adjusted EBITDA beat Wall Street’s consensus estimates by 16.2%.
Free cash flow

Adjusted EBITDA shows how profitable a company’s existing “rock” is before financing and reinvestment, while free cash flow shows how much value remains after paying to replace those wells. Because production declines over time, strong EBITDA can coexist with weak FCF if drilling is expensive or declines are steep. FCF therefore captures both operating efficiency and the cost of sustaining production.

SLB has shown decent cash profitability, giving it some flexibility to reinvest or return capital to investors. The company’s free cash flow margin averaged 9.7% over the last five years, slightly better than the broader energy upstream and integrated energy sector.
The level of free cash flow is important, but its durability across cycles is just as critical. Consistent margins are far more valuable than volatile swings driven by commodity prices.

SLB’s ratio of quarterly free cash flow volatility to WTI crude price volatility over the past five years was 6.5 (lower is better), indicating that its cash generation is relatively insulated from swings in commodity prices compared with most peers. This resilience supports access to capital in downturns and positions the company to act as a consolidator when distressed assets come to market at attractive prices.

Why use free cash flow to assess stability against commodity prices rather than compare revenue or EBITDA to WTI crude prices in SLB’s case? Because what ultimately matters is not how much revenue or profit a company earns when prices are high but how much cash it can generate when prices are low. Free cash flow is the superior metric because it includes everything from hedging effectiveness to growth and maintenance capex to management behavior during good times and bad.

children: SLB’s free cash flow totaled $1.03 billion in Q3, equivalent to a 10.8% margin. The company’s cash profitability declined as it was 1.5 percentage points lower than in the same quarter last year, but it’s still above its five-year average. It is important not to read too much into this quarter’s decline because investment needs can be seasonal, causing short-term swings. Long-term trends carry greater meaning.
Key takeaways from SLB’s Q3 results

SLB’s revenue and EPS both topped Wall Street’s consensus estimates, giving the quarter some clear positives and making it a decent showing overall. Shares remained flat at $49.71 immediately after the results.

SLB reported solid earnings, but one quarter doesn’t necessarily make the stock a buy. To assess the investment, consider the bigger picture of valuation and business quality as well as the latest earnings.
